issues.legal_issue: A business conducted by a member of a Hindu joint family is not joint family property merely because its proprietor is a family member or manager.
material_facts: The business was started by one family member after he took over a pre-existing business and its assets in his own right.
The other family members had little income and the family lacked sufficient funds to contribute to the business when it began.
The courts below found no evidence that joint family property or funds assisted the business or that the business was treated as a family business.
Documents and correspondence generally described the person who started the business as its proprietor.
issues.conclusion: The business was the separate business of its proprietor, not a joint family business, and the claim to partition its assets was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Hindu law creates no presumption that a business standing in a family member’s name is a joint family business, even if that member manages the family. The party asserting joint family character must establish assistance from joint family property or funds, or blending of the business earnings with the joint family estate; whether such assistance or treatment occurred is a question of fact. The Court relied on Bhuru Mal v. Jagannath, AIR 1943 PC 40; Pearey Lai v. Nanak Chand, AIR 1948 PC 108; and Chattanatha Karayalar v. Ramachandra Iyer, AIR 1955 SC 799.

predicates.business_claimed_as_joint_family_propert: A party claims that a business conducted by a family member belongs to the joint family.
predicates.no_joint_family_funds_assisted_business: Joint family property or funds did not assist in starting or carrying on the business.
predicates.business_earnings_not_blended_with_famil: The business earnings were not blended with the joint family estate.

issues.definition: If a business is claimed as joint family property but received no assistance from joint family funds and its earnings were not blended with the family estate, the business remains separate property.

issues.legal_issue: A coparcener’s separate property becomes joint family property only upon a clear intention to relinquish separate rights, not through physical mixing or ambiguous descriptions alone.
material_facts: The business had been started and conducted as the proprietor’s separate business.
Documents and communications continued to describe him as the proprietor, and he conducted himself as the sole proprietor.

Some instruments described the business or property as being for family benefit, but the courts found those recitals could have been made to obtain loans and did not establish an intention to surrender separate rights.
The claimant did not establish that the proprietor intended to place the business in the common stock.
issues.conclusion: The business was not converted into joint family property because there was no clear intention by its proprietor to relinquish his separate rights.
issues.legal_principle: Separate property of a Hindu coparcener acquires the character of joint family or ancestral property through the coparcener’s volition and intention to waive or surrender the special right in it, not by mere physical mixing. The intention must be established; mere recitals or dealings describing self-acquired property as joint family property are not by themselves sufficient. The Court relied on Hurpurshad v. Sheo Dyal, 3 I.A. 219; Lal Bahadur v. Kanhaiya Lal, 34 I.A. 65; Lola Muddun Gopal v. Khikhinda Koeri, 18 I.A. 9; and Naina Pilla v. Daiyanai Ammal, AIR 1936 Mad 177.

predicates.property_began_as_separate_property: The property was originally acquired or conducted as one coparcener’s separate property.
predicates.clear_intent_to_relinquish_separate_righ: The coparcener clearly intended to waive or surrender his separate rights in the property.

issues.definition: When property began as separate property and its owner did not clearly intend to relinquish separate rights, it does not become joint family property.

issues.legal_issue: A family member’s labor in a separate business does not by itself establish that the member is a co-owner.
material_facts: The claimant joined the business after it had been started by his brother.
A contemporaneous application described the claimant as a clerk and his brother as the proprietor; other documents also described the brother as proprietor.
The claimant did not establish when or how his status changed from employee to co-owner, or that he asserted co-ownership during his brother’s lifetime.
The evidence showed that the claimant acted in the business under authority given by his brother.
issues.conclusion: The claimant’s work in the business did not make him a co-owner, and his co-ownership claim was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no basis to infer co-ownership from the claimant’s work where the evidence described him as an employee or authorized agent and did not show an agreement, assertion, or recognition of ownership. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited on this issue.

predicates.family_member_worked_in_business: A family member performed work in a business owned or operated by another family member.
predicates.worked_as_employee_or_agent: The family member worked as an employee or acted under the proprietor’s authority.
predicates.no_evidence_of_agreement_or_recognition: There was no evidence that the proprietor agreed to co-ownership or recognized the family member as a co-owner.

issues.definition: When a family member worked in another’s business as an employee or agent, or there was no evidence of an agreement or recognition of ownership, the work alone does not establish co-ownership.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not re-examine a concurrent factual finding in a civil appeal when the finding is not shown to be legally vitiated.
material_facts: Both lower courts found that the business was separate and was neither a joint family business nor treated as one.
The appellant argued that the finding was legally defective because certain documents had not been considered.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had examined the documents and that the appellant had not shown the concurrent factual finding to be legally vitiated.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the business was separate was not open to further scrutiny in the appeal and was left undisturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Following the usual practice under Article 133 of the Constitution, the Court does not further scrutinize a concurrent finding of fact in a civil appeal where no legal defect has been established.

predicates.civil_appeal_from_concurrent_factual_fin: The proceeding is a civil appeal in which both lower courts reached the same factual finding.
predicates.finding_not_legally_vitiated: The appellant has not established that the concurrent factual finding is legally defective.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal from a concurrent factual finding that has not been shown to be legally defective, the Supreme Court does not re-examine that finding.
